newsitem.title: USA: US CREDIT OUTLOOK - 10-yr Treasury note auction.
newsitem.headline: US CREDIT OUTLOOK - 10-yr Treasury note auction.

text.p: With the first leg of the Treasury's $39.75 billion three-part quarterly refinancing behind it, the market shifts its focus to the Treasury sale of $12.0 billion in 10-year notes on Wednesday.
The Treasury sold $17.75 billion in three-year notes on Tuesday in an auction that the market was able to absorb with relative ease.
There is little to distract the market's attention from the 10-year Treasury note sale on Wednesday.

The only economic data due before the 1300 EST/1800 GMT bidding deadline for the 10-year auction is the index of the Federal Reserve Bank of Atlanta. No forecast was available for the January index. But the December gauge of business activity in the Atlanta area read -14.6.
Market participants said the 10-year note auction would probably proceed smoothly.

"So far, so good," said Kevin Sluder, head government trader at First Chicago Capital Markets Inc. "The three-year auction was slightly weak, but certainly not dramatically weak and didn't set a precedent for the rest of the refunding."
After the Treasury sells 10-year notes on Wednesday, it is scheduled to sell $10.0 billion in 30-year bonds on Thursday.
One variable with the potential to alter the view of the auction is the dollar's performance overnight, traders said.
"Everybody definitely has one eye on the dollar for the next few days," said Sluder.

In late New York trade on Tuesday, the dollar retained small gains after an early rally. Wariness of potential central bank dollar selling after the G7 meeting in Berlin last weekend checked the advance of the U.S. unit.
The concern in the financial markets is that a reversal of the dollar's ascent could translate into weaker foreign demand for U.S. financial assets.
In afternoon when-issued trade on Tuesday, the 10-year notes to be sold on Wednesday were yielding 6.3775 percent.

"Between now and tomorrow, the market could push the yield on the when-issued 10-years toward 6.40 percent," said Larry Pavelec, director of fixed-income and the manager of the Milwaukee, Wisc.-based Marshall Government Income Fund. "That's not a big deal. I think we'll do better after the refunding auctions end."

One question raised regarding the 10-year note sale is the amount of supply at that sector of the maturity curve. The Treasury now auctions inflation-indexed 10-year notes four times a year besides the six auctions a year at which it sells regular 10-year notes, said Sluder.
But participants said chances were good that the market could absorb all that supply, even with the concentration of securities at the 10-year sector.
"There's some validity to the notion that there's a bubble of supply there, but I think you have a different buyer for the 10-year inflation-indexed notes," said Pavelec.

Carey Leahey, senior vice president and senior economist at Lehman Government Securities Inc., said taking notice of the supply in the 10-year area was reasonable, but he said there is also demand for that maturity.
"Ten-years are the No. 1 maturity for hedging," said Leahey, noting ample corporate supply to hedge against.
He, too, theorized that inflation-indexed notes are bought by a different kind of buyer and are less liquid.

"The experience has been in other markets that have traded inflation-indexed bonds is that they're scooped up and kept," said Leahy. "They don't contribute to liquidity that much. There's some market segmentation. A different set of investors buys the 10-year as an inflation hedge so they're illiquid."
Dealers indicated that Federal funds would open between 5-3/8 percent and 5-1/2 percent on Wednesday.
On Tuesday, the benchmark 30-year Treasury bond finished at 97-11/12, down 1/32, to yield 6.71 percent.
-- (( North American Treasury Desk 212-859-1679))
